questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't a simple yes/no CDE identification test (Lesson 16) enough on its own?
options: A real organization can have more identified CDEs than it can govern with equal intensity, so they need to be ranked
Because the yes/no test from Lesson 16 is always wrong
Because CDEs automatically lose their status after 90 days
Because only one CDE is allowed per organization
questions.explain: Forty CDEs is common at a mid-sized company — at that point the question shifts from 'is this critical' to 'which one needs attention first.'

questions.q: What are the two independent axes this lesson uses to score and rank CDEs?
options: Impact and likelihood of error
Table size and column count
Alphabetical order and creation date
Storage cost and backup frequency
questions.explain: Impact measures how bad it is if the element is wrong; likelihood measures how probable it is the element is currently wrong, given its source and validation.

questions.q: In the worked ranking, why did TaxRate get a lower priority than OrderTotal despite both having high impact?
options: TaxRate has a lower likelihood of error, since it's sourced from a single validated reference table
TaxRate is not actually a Critical Data Element at all
OrderTotal has no impact score at all
TaxRate's column name is longer than OrderTotal's
questions.explain: Both elements score high on impact, but TaxRate's low likelihood of error (coming from a validated source) pulls its overall priority down relative to OrderTotal's medium likelihood.

questions.q: Why did SalesRepNotes rank as low priority in the worked example, even though it has a high likelihood of containing errors?
options: Because its impact is low — it's informational only and feeds no calculations
Because free-text fields can never be Critical Data Elements by definition
Because it was the most recently created column
Because SalesRepNotes has no likelihood score at all
questions.explain: A high likelihood of error doesn't outweigh low impact — prioritization requires both dimensions to point toward real governance value, not just error-proneness alone.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what typically changes once an element is ranked as a high-priority CDE?
options: It gets a named accountable owner, scheduled data quality rules, a documented remediation process, and a shorter review cycle
It is immediately deleted from the database for safety
Nothing changes in practice — ranking is purely documentation with no operational effect
It is automatically converted into a business glossary term
questions.explain: Ranking determines where real governance effort gets spent — high-priority CDEs get elevated ownership, monitoring, and review cadence that lower-priority elements don't.
